note: Every way a generated page may point INSIDE a file, and what it means. Written by hand, per webview/conformance/README.md: a vector is a claim about behaviour, and generating it from one implementation would only prove that implementation agrees with itself. The page side (scripts/webview-location) and the host side (webview-core) both assert against this file.
grammar: A fragment is the part after '#' in a link, without the '#'. One leading '#' is tolerated and stripped.

'L<line>' and 'L<from>-L<to>' are explicit positions and always win, and a position may name the column it starts at after a colon ('L42:12'). Lines and columns count from 1 and a range may not end before it starts, as the reference implementation reads them: '#L0' and '#L58-L42' are malformed, not clamped. A range carries the column it starts at; its END column is not carried, because this contract places one caret and selects a line span.

'<ref>' names a region or a declaration, with inject-examples' scope modifiers '-' (body only), '+' (with annotations) and '++' (with annotations and the doc comment). The reference implementation owns that spelling, and in its current grammar a modifier is a whole TRAILING segment: 'add/-', 'add/+', 'add/++'. The older leading forms ('+add', '++add') are refused by it, and '-add' is not a modifier at all but a name, because '-' may appear in a name and '+' may not.
In a .json file the reference is a comma-separated list of dotted key paths, because JSON has no comments to hang a region on.
A bare name is a declaration in a source file, and a heading anchor in a document (.md, .markdown, .html, .htm) - which is why a link to '#install' in a README is left to the page itself.

The reference also reads a comma as a list of selectors and an envelope pair ('foo/^,foo/$'). A list is several places and an envelope is a property of one, so neither is one location in this contract: they are not locations here, and the file opens instead. A .json file's comma list is its own rule, checked before the reference, and is unaffected.
Anything else is not a location and stays an ordinary link.

cases.why: the maintainer's example: a method inside a source file
an explicit line, the spelling the JetBrains host resolves today
a range, which the host selects rather than a caret
a one-line range is still a range: the page asked for a selection
line 0 is malformed rather than line 1: the reference implementation counts lines and columns from 1, so a page that wrote it has a bug, not a clamp
a reversed range is malformed too - the reference refuses it ('ends before it starts') rather than normalising what the page wrote
an open-ended range is not a location
a position may name the column it starts at: line 42 from its twelfth character, which a caret can be placed at (the page splits on ':' and needs no grammar for it)
and a range carries the column it starts at; its end column is not carried, because a caret is one position and the selection is a line span
a leading '#' is tolerated, because a page has the fragment either way
a declaration or a region, by bare name
the body only: the modifier is the path's last segment, which is the spelling the reference implementation reads
the declaration and its annotations
the declaration, annotations and doc comment - the form the resolver docs use
a bare plus is refused by the reference implementation, which says so and names the spelling to use ('#<path>/+'): reading it as a region would be a second grammar beside it
and the same for the widening double plus, which used to be the resolver docs' spelling
a plus glued to a name is not a modifier either
a trailing minus is NOT a modifier: '-' may appear in a name, so 'add-' is the name it says
and a leading minus is a name character too, so this is a name and never a body-only region
two or three minus signs are names as well - there is no such modifier, and the name is what the page wrote
and the three-minus spelling is a name for the same reason
a reference may be a path - 'Cart/add' is the spelling the webview README names - so the name a link carries is the path it wrote
and the scope rides on the end of that path
a minus after the slash is a name inside the path, not a modifier: only the LAST segment may be one, and '-add' is not a modifier spelling
a bare modifier names nothing
the reference reads a comma as a list of selectors; this contract names one place, and a .json file's comma list is its own rule
an envelope pair is a property of a reference list, not one place in this contract
regions exist in every file type, markdown included
in .json the reference is the JSON rule: one dotted key path
and the JSON rule takes a list, which is why the two rules are told apart by the file's type
whitespace around the keys is the writer's formatting, not part of a key
an array element is a dotted path like any other
in .json a bare reference is the JSON rule before the reference grammar: JSON has no regions, and a leading dash is a legal key character

a bare fragment in a document is a candidate too: the page scrolls to a heading of that name without asking anyone, and only asks a host when the name is not one - which is how a README region link works
and a document takes a scope the same way a source file does: the modifier is the last segment
and the same is true of HTML, whose anchors are its own
but an explicit line in a document is still a location
a nested or qualified declaration name is a member like any other
a scheme-like fragment is not a location; a colon is never part of a reference
a declaration needs a file type to be told from a heading anchor, so no path means no member
an explicit position needs no file type at all
and neither is an empty fragment: the file itself, which needs no navigation

THE maintainer's case: a bare name spelled like a region, with no prefix at all - it is a name exactly like a method or a field, and what it resolves to is the host's business (a declaration, or a #region directive of that name)
a name that may contain a dash reads as the name it is, whatever the dash count
the widening double plus, in the spelling the reference reads
in .json there are no declarations to find, so a bare reference is the JSON rule: dotted key paths
a list in a code file is not one location in this contract, while the same text in .json is its key list
